title: Vocabulary: Words Associated with Animal Husbandry
summary: Words for types of animal farming, animal housing, the people who look after animals and their health, and breeding and feeding.

p: Animal husbandry is the branch of agriculture that deals with the care, breeding, rearing and management of domesticated animals. They give us food (meat, milk and eggs), materials (wool and leather) and services (transport and farm labour). The field has special words for the animals, their homes, their health and how they are raised.
Learn these terms and use them in your own sentences.

head: Word
Meaning
Example sentence
rows: Domesticated animals raised for profit or use, especially cattle, sheep, goats and pigs
The farmer's livestock included 50 cows and 100 goats.
Domesticated birds (chickens, turkeys, ducks, geese) raised for eggs or meat
Poultry farming is profitable because of the high demand for eggs.
The branch of farming that raises pigs
He built a clean piggery to prevent diseases.
The branch of farming that produces milk and milk products such as cheese and yoghurt
Dairy cows must be milked twice a day.
Fish farming, or the industry of catching fish
The coastal town's economy depends on its fishery.
A place where bees are kept in hives for honey
An apiary needs special knowledge of bee behaviour.

p: Different animals live in different places.

head: Word
Meaning
Example sentence
rows: A small fenced enclosure for animals such as goats, pigs or sheep
The goats are kept in a wooden pen behind the house.
A small cage or house for poultry
He cleaned the chicken coop every morning.
A building where horses are kept and fed
The racehorse was resting in its stable.
Land covered with grass and plants where animals such as cattle and sheep graze
The herdsman led the cows to the green pasture.
A small field or enclosure, usually near a stable, where horses are kept
The horses were running in the paddock.

p: Herdsman: a person who owns or looks after a herd of livestock, usually cattle. Shepherd: a person who looks after sheep. Vet (veterinary doctor): an animal doctor who diagnoses, treats and prevents animal diseases. Vaccination: giving an animal a vaccine to stop it getting a particular disease (Vaccination of day-old chicks is compulsory).

Breeding: causing animals to produce young, often to develop certain qualities (Selective breeding has produced cows that give more milk). Grazing: animals eating grass directly from the pasture. Feed: prepared food given to farm animals (The farmer bought ten bags of poultry feed). Fodder: dried food such as hay or straw used as animal feed. Incubator: a heated container used to hatch eggs artificially (The incubator allows the farm to hatch 500 eggs at once).

title: Spoken English: Consonants Followed by /j/
summary: The /j/ ('y') glide after consonants, the clusters /pj/, /bj/, /kj/, /mj/, /fj/, /vj/, /hj/, and the British and American difference called yod-dropping.

p: The symbol /j/ does not stand for the letter j. It is the 'y' sound at the beginning of yes /jes/. It is a glide, or semi-vowel: the tongue starts high and near the front of the mouth (as for /iː/) and moves to the next vowel.
/j/ often follows a consonant to make a 'consonant + y' blend. Music is not 'moo-zik'. It is /ˈmjuːzɪk/ ('myoo-zik').
Learn these words and say each one aloud.
The /j/ is sometimes called the 'yod'. British English and standard Nigerian English keep the /j/. American English tends to drop it after /t/, /d/ and /n/. This is called yod-dropping.
Examples: tune: British /tjuːn/, American /tuːn/. due: /djuː/ and /duː/. new: /njuː/ and /nuː/. Tuesday: /ˈtjuːzdeɪ/ and /ˈtuːzdeɪ/. student: /ˈstjuːdənt/ and /ˈstuːdənt/.
For WAEC and NECO, you are expected to know and use the British pronunciation, with the /j/.
Say these words clearly: music, beauty, pure, cure, few, view, huge; Tuesday, student, new, duty, endure, tune.

Sentences (use the British pronunciation): The new student had a huge sense of humour. It is his duty to play music every Tuesday. The beautiful view was a cure for his bad mood. Are you curious about the new computer?

title: Continuous Writing: Descriptive Essay, 'A Fire Incident in My Street'
summary: Narrative versus description, a sensory bank for a fire scene, similes, metaphors and personification, and a full sample essay.

p: A descriptive composition paints a picture with words so that the reader feels as if they are at the scene. A fire is a powerful topic because it is full of strong sensations.

A narrative tells the story of the fire: First it started, then the firemen came, finally it was over. A description focuses on the experience: The heat was scorching, the smoke was choking and the sounds were terrifying.

sections.h: The sensory bank for a fire
p: Collect your words before you write.

head: Sense
Details
rows: thick, black, billowing smoke; angry orange and red flames; glowing embers; flashing lights of fire engines; terrified faces; people running; cracked walls; shattered glass; the skeleton of a burnt building
screams of Help and Fire; the crackling and popping of burning wood; shattering glass; the roar of the fire; sirens; shouting firefighters; weeping
acrid smoke; burning plastic and rubber; scorched wood; singed hair; a choking smell that burns the nostrils
unbearable heat; stinging smoke in the eyes; hot tears; spray from a fire hose; the push of a panicked crowd; a pounding heart
panic, chaos, fear, despair, sadness, shock

p: Simile: The smoke rose like a dark giant. The flames danced like angry spears. Metaphor: The fire was a raging monster. The building was a burning skeleton. Personification: The fire devoured the house. Flames licked at the windows. The siren screamed.

sections.h: Sample composition: The Day the Street Burned
p: It was a hot, dry Sunday afternoon, and the air was still. Suddenly the peace was shattered by a woman's high-pitched scream: 'Fire! Fire!' I ran outside and froze. Thick, black smoke was billowing into the sky from Mr Kalu's shop, just three houses down. The smoke was a dark monster, blocking out the sun.

Within minutes, the scene descended into chaos. People ran in panic, some carrying children, others holding useless buckets of water. Then we saw the flames. They were not small; they were angry, orange tongues that licked greedily at the sky. The heat was intense, even from my spot, and it pushed us back. We heard the terrifying crackle of the fire as it devoured the building's wooden roof, followed by the shattering of glass as the windows exploded.

The stench was unbearable, a choking mix of burning plastic and scorched wood. Women were crying and men were shouting uselessly. When the fire engine's siren wailed in the distance, it was the most beautiful sound I had ever heard. Firefighters began battling the raging beast with powerful jets of water. After what felt like an eternity, the fire was put out, leaving the blackened, skeletal ruins of what used to be a home. Though no one died, the street was silent, shocked by the speed of the destruction.

title: Grammar: Irregular Verbs
summary: Regular and irregular verbs, the three forms (base, past tense, past participle), and the main groups of irregular verbs with examples.

p: Regular verbs follow a fixed rule: add -d or -ed for the past tense and the past participle (walk, walked, walked; love, loved, loved). Irregular verbs do not follow this rule. Their forms change in unpredictable ways and have to be learned by heart.

The three forms: the base form (eat), the past tense, used for finished actions (I ate yesterday), and the past participle, used with helper (auxiliary) verbs such as has, have, had, was and were to form perfect and passive tenses (I have eaten; It was eaten).
All three forms are the same.

sections.h: Group 2: past and past participle are the same
p: The vowel changes, but the second and third forms match.

sections.h: Group 3: all three forms are different (i, a, u)
p: The vowel changes from i to a to u.

sections.h: Group 4: the past participle ends in -en
p: These end in -n or -en in the past participle.
Be: am, is, are; was, were; been. Go: went, gone. Do: did, done.

Using the past tense where the past participle is needed. Past tense: I went to the market yesterday. Past participle: I have gone to the market already. Wrong: She has wrote the letter. Right: She has written the letter. Wrong: The glass was broke. Right: The glass was broken.

title: Spoken English: The /j/ Sound, the Long Vowel /uː/ and the Short Vowel /ʊ/
summary: How to make /j/ and /uː/, the difference between the long /uː/ (pool) and the short /ʊ/ (pull), and how the sounds combine in words like due, new and music.

p: /j/ is the sound of the letter y in yes. It is a semi-vowel made by raising the front and middle of the tongue high towards the hard palate, but not so close that it causes friction. After a consonant it makes a blend, as shown below.

In some accents, especially American, the yod is dropped after /t/, /d/ and /n/. Tune: British /tjuːn/ (tyoon), American /tuːn/ (toon). Due: British /djuː/, American /duː/. New: British /njuː/, American /nuː/. For WAEC and NECO, use the British pronunciation with the /j/.
This is the long 'oo' sound. The back of the tongue is high and the lips are tightly rounded. Examples: food, blue, true, school, fruit, rule, June, move, group.
The short /ʊ/ (as in pull) has less rounded lips and is much shorter. This pair is tested often, so practise the minimal pairs.
Many words combine the two sounds: due = /d/ + /j/ + /uː/ = /djuː/. stew = /s/ + /t/ + /j/ + /uː/ = /stjuː/. new = /n/ + /j/ + /uː/ = /njuː/. music = /m/ + /j/ + /uː/ + /zɪk/ = /ˈmjuːzɪk/.

title: Listening Comprehension: A Short Debate
summary: What a debate is, how to listen for main arguments and evidence, signal words, and a short debate on television and students.

p: A debate is a formal, structured argument between two sides about a topic called the motion. The proposition (the 'for' side) agrees with the motion. The opposition (the 'against' side) disagrees with it.
As a listener your job is not to be persuaded but to be an analyst: to listen carefully to what each side says and how they say it.
Focus on main arguments: what is each speaker's main reason? Listen for evidence: do they use facts, numbers or examples, or just feelings?
Listen for signal words. To introduce points: my first point is, secondly, furthermore. To disagree: my opponent said, however, on the contrary. To conclude: in conclusion, therefore, I urge you to.
Take notes in a T-chart: draw a line down the middle of the page, FOR on the left and AGAINST on the right, and write the points under each.
Motion: Television does more harm than good to students.

Speaker A (proposition, for): Good morning. The motion is clear: television does more harm than good, and I strongly agree. My first point is that television is a major cause of poor academic performance. It is addictive. Students spend hours watching movies and music videos instead of reading their books or doing their homework. Secondly, television exposes children to violence and values that are not part of our culture. They see crime and bad behaviour and think it is normal. In conclusion, television is a dangerous distraction that harms our students.

Speaker B (opposition, against): My opponent has painted a very one-sided picture. On the contrary, television is one of the most powerful tools for education. Where else can a student watch live documentaries about wildlife in the Amazon, or see the inside of a volcano? Furthermore, television connects us to the world. We learn about global events and politics from news channels. It provides information and relaxation. The problem is not the television; the problem is a lack of discipline and parental guidance. Therefore, I urge you to reject this motion.

The motion: television does more harm than good to students. Main argument of Speaker A: television causes poor academic performance (and exposes children to violence). Main argument of Speaker B: television is a powerful educational tool that also connects us to the world. B's supporting example: documentaries about wildlife in the Amazon or the inside of a volcano. B's signal words: for disagreement, 'on the contrary' and 'my opponent has painted a very one-sided picture'; for an added point, 'furthermore'. Which speaker is more persuasive depends on the arguments: A gives clear reasons, but B gives concrete examples and points out the real cause of the problem.

title: Reading Comprehension: Identifying Main Ideas
summary: Topic, main idea and supporting details, how to find the topic sentence, with a passage on Nigeria's resources and a practice passage on social media.

p: Every passage has one central message the author wants you to understand. That is the main idea, the big picture or the main reason the author wrote it. The topic is what the passage is about (one or two words). The main idea is the most important point the author makes about the topic (a full sentence). Supporting details are the facts, examples and reasons that prove or explain the main idea.

sections.h: How to find the main idea
p: 1. Read the title and skim the passage to find the topic.
2. Read carefully and look for the topic sentence, the one sentence that summarises the whole paragraph. It is often the first or last sentence.
3. Look for repeated words or ideas, which give clues.
4. Ask yourself: what is the one thing the author wants me to know about this topic?

Nigeria is blessed with many natural resources such as crude oil, coal and limestone. However, corruption and mismanagement have prevented the nation from fully benefiting from these resources. If citizens show honesty and accountability, the country's economy will improve greatly.

Topic: Nigeria's resources and economy. Supporting detail: Nigeria has crude oil, coal and limestone. Supporting detail: citizens should show honesty. Main idea: Nigeria's economic problem is not a lack of resources, but a lack of good management caused by corruption.

Social media has fundamentally changed how we communicate. Platforms like Instagram, X (formerly Twitter) and TikTok allow instant connection with people across the world. They can be powerful tools for business, education and social movements. However, this constant connection has a downside. Studies have shown that excessive social media use can lead to anxiety, depression and poor sleep patterns. It can also spread misinformation at a very fast rate. Therefore, users must be mindful and learn to balance their online and offline lives.

Topic: social media. Main idea: social media is a powerful tool with both significant benefits and serious dangers, so users must be careful. Positive effects: instant connection, and use for business, education and social movements. Negative effects: anxiety, depression, poor sleep, fast spread of false information. Advice in the last sentence: balance online and offline life.

title: Grammar: Irregular Verbs (Continued)
summary: Past tense and past participle again, with helper verbs, three more groups, and the most common error.

p: A regular verb forms its past tense by adding -ed (walk, walked). An irregular verb does not follow this rule; it changes its form, often by changing its vowel. There are three key forms. The base form (present) is the basic verb: eat, go, see. The past tense is used for a finished action and stands alone: I went to the market yesterday. The past participle is used with a helper (auxiliary) verb such as has, have, had, was or were: I have gone to the market; The food was eaten.

The most common error is using the past tense where the past participle is needed. Wrong: She has wrote the letter. Right: She has written the letter. Wrong: The glass was broke. Right: The glass was broken. Remember: after has, have, had, was or were, you need the past participle.

sections.h: Group 1: all three forms different (i, a, u)
p: Learn these by heart.
Many of these verbs follow the pattern of base, past (no -en) and participle (with -en).

sections.h: Group 3: past and past participle are the same
p: These are easy because only the base is different.
She has (begin) to read the book. (begun)
The boy (run) home from school yesterday. (ran)
We (see) that film last week. (saw)
The song was (sing) by the choir. (sung)
I have (eat) all my food. (eaten)
